headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared MCP/file workflows; compliance risk is moderate due to document data handling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents expose MCP surfaces and process external content: agent_a uses MCP/stdio and stdin/stdout, while agent_b exposes an MCP Server and ingests PDFs/DOCX/XLSX. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if A forwards or transforms untrusted content into B’s parsing path. No direct provenance controls are documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards untrusted text into agent_b's MCP or file-processing inputs, injection becomes reachable.
IF either agent treats parsed document text as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer downstream behavior.
mitigations: Disable MCP bridging between the agents for untrusted inputs.
Insert a strict content-type gate before any handoff from A to B.
Strip instructions-like prefixes from extracted text before reuse.
Log and review all cross-agent payloads for prompt markers.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to every transferred artifact.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures; agent_b processes PDFs, images, DOCX, XLSX, and OCR text. Both have allowlisted network egress and MCP/API surfaces, so a shared workspace or handoff could leak sensitive document or repository data into outputs or remote calls. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this is not high.
conditions: IF the two agents share a workspace or exchange files, sensitive content can cross boundaries.
IF agent_b uploads extracted document text to its backend, data from agent_a-fed files can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep the agents in separate directories or containers.
Avoid passing raw documents from A to B unless redacted.
Turn off network egress for test runs where possible.
Review outputs for secrets before export.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent_a can execute shell commands, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b cannot write files or modify git, but it does support concurrent inference and MCP/API access. The main conflict is not symmetric write contention, but A can mutate shared repo state while B concurrently reads or processes artifacts, creating race conditions and inconsistent outputs. Uncertainty about shared storage keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository checkout, A can change state while B reads stale artifacts.
IF B is configured to consume files produced by A concurrently, inconsistent parses or partial reads can occur.
mitigations: Run the agents on separate checkouts.
Serialize any git-mutating step from agent_a.
Use read-only mounts for agent_b inputs.
Pause B while A is writing artifacts.
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared workspaces.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a can generate or transform content via shell/MCP workflows, and agent_b is a document-processing system that can ingest extracted text and structured outputs. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream documents or actions. There is no documented verification layer between them, so the safer medium classification applies.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without validation, any upstream mistake propagates downstream.
IF A produces malformed structured text, B may render or extract it as if it were factual.
mitigations: Add a human review step before B consumes A output.
Require schema validation on A-to-B handoffs.
Compare extracted facts against source documents.
Reject outputs containing unresolved placeholders.
requires-engineering: implement confidence/provenance checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_b is explicitly a document processor handling PDFs, images, DOCX, XLSX, OCR text, while agent_a touches task prompts, repository metadata, and code. If regulated or personal documents flow through B and are then combined with A’s broader repo/task context, retention or residency mismatches can arise. The profiles do not show HIPAA/GDPR certifications, so the risk is compliance drift rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated documents are processed by agent_b and then stored or re-exported through agent_a workflows, retention controls may diverge.
IF the deployment requires specific residency or certification guarantees, neither profile documents them.
mitigations: Classify documents before processing.
Keep regulated data out of mixed-agent workflows.
Document retention and deletion rules for both agents.
Verify residency and certification claims before deployment.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing.
